blocks.text: Hugging Face Transformers is the most widely used open source library for working with pretrained language models, providing a consistent interface to load, run, and fine-tune thousands of publicly available models without writing model architecture code from scratch.

This topic covers the core pieces of the library relevant to fine-tuning, model loading, tokenization, and the Trainer API, along with where it fits alongside the other frameworks covered later in this module.
1. What Transformers Provides

blocks.alt: The Model Hub connects through the Transformers library into your project

blocks.text: The library gives a single, consistent Python interface for working with a huge range of pretrained models hosted on the Hugging Face Model Hub, so switching between different model architectures or checkpoints usually requires changing only a model name string, not rewriting your code.
2. Loading a Pretrained Model

blocks.alt: Pretrained weights are loaded through from_pretrained into a loaded model

blocks.text: The from_pretrained method is the library core entry point, downloading and loading both a model architecture and its pretrained weights with a single call, the same pattern works whether the model has a few hundred million parameters or tens of billions.

code.content:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_name = "meta-llama/Llama-3-8b"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)

blocks.text: 3. The Tokenizer

blocks.alt: Raw text goes through a tokenizer to become token IDs

blocks.text: Every model ships with a matching tokenizer, covered in more general terms in an earlier topic, that converts raw text into the specific token ID sequence that model expects, using the exact same tokenizer a model was pretrained with is essential, a mismatched tokenizer silently produces garbage results.
4. The Trainer API

blocks.alt: A dataset and TrainingArguments feed into the Trainer, producing a fine-tuned model

blocks.text: The Trainer class wraps the standard training loop, forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, optimizer step, logging, checkpointing, behind a high level interface configured through a TrainingArguments object, letting a fine-tuning run be launched with only a few dozen lines of setup code.

code.content:
from transformers import TrainingArguments, Trainer

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./output",
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    learning_rate=2e-5,
)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=dataset)
trainer.train()

blocks.text: 5. Trainer API vs a Custom Training Loop

blocks.alt: The high level Trainer API is compared against a custom training loop with full control

blocks.text: The Trainer API handles the common case well and saves substantial boilerplate, but some advanced or unusual training setups need finer grained control than its configuration options expose, in those cases, writing a custom training loop directly with the underlying model and PyTorch primitives remains fully possible and sometimes necessary.

blocks.text: 6. Ecosystem Integration

blocks.alt: Transformers connects to PEFT, Accelerate, and TRL

blocks.text: Transformers is designed to work directly with several companion libraries covered later in this module, PEFT for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Accelerate for distributed and mixed precision training, and TRL for preference optimization methods like DPO and PPO, all covered in earlier topics, rather than needing separate, incompatible tooling for each.

blocks.title: The library ecosystem is a major reason for its popularity
blocks.content: Because PEFT, Accelerate, and TRL all build directly on top of Transformers core abstractions, a fine-tuning pipeline can mix and match these tools without needing to reconcile incompatible model or data representations.

blocks.text: 7. Model Architecture Code vs Pretrained Weights

blocks.alt: Model architecture code is distinct from the pretrained weights download

blocks.text: It helps to understand that Transformers ships two separable things for each supported model, the architecture code itself, which is open source and inspectable, and the pretrained weights, which are downloaded separately from the Hub, understanding this separation matters when debugging or when working with a custom model variant.
8. Community and Model Availability

The Model Hub hosts an enormous and constantly growing number of community-contributed checkpoints, including many already fine-tuned for specific tasks, often a useful starting point is checking whether a close match to your task already exists before fine-tuning entirely from scratch.
9. When to Reach for Transformers

Transformers is close to a default choice for most fine-tuning work in this course, its main tradeoffs against more specialized frameworks like Unsloth or Axolotl, both covered in later topics, tend to be around ease of use and speed for common recipes versus the greater flexibility Transformers itself provides.
Worked Example

A team wants to fine-tune an open source model for a classification task. Using Transformers, they load a pretrained model and its matching tokenizer with two from_pretrained calls, prepare their dataset, and configure a TrainingArguments object specifying batch size, epochs, and learning rate.

Handing all of this to a Trainer instance and calling train lets them launch a full fine-tuning run without writing a manual training loop, and because the setup follows the library standard interface, switching to a different base model later only requires changing the model name string.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a tokenizer that does not match the loaded model, producing silently broken results
Reaching immediately for a custom training loop when the Trainer API configuration options would have covered the need
Not checking the Model Hub for an existing fine-tuned checkpoint before starting a fine-tuning run from scratch
Ignoring the companion libraries, PEFT, Accelerate, and TRL, that integrate directly with Transformers for more specialized needs

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning task you are familiar with, sketch out the from_pretrained calls, TrainingArguments settings, and Trainer setup you would need, and identify which companion library from this topic, PEFT, Accelerate, or TRL, your specific task would most likely also require.
Key Takeaway

Hugging Face Transformers provides a consistent interface for loading pretrained models and tokenizers and, through the Trainer API, running standard fine-tuning workflows with minimal boilerplate, forming the foundation that companion libraries like PEFT, Accelerate, and TRL, all covered in this module, build directly on top of.
